skill.name: A setting built from the senses
skill.why: Readers can't see your world. Senses let them step inside it.
skill.how: Pick a place. Add what you'd hear, smell, touch and taste, not just see.

steps.say: My first try at describing the school canteen.

show.text: The canteen was big and had lots of tables.

steps.ask: Which sense does my line use?

options.reason: Is there any noise in it? Read it again.
Nothing smells in it. There is just big and tables.

steps.win: Right. Only sight. You're not in there yet.

steps.say: I added more. Listen, sniff and feel.

show.text: The canteen hummed with kids slurping noodles.
The air stank of burnt toast.
show.nudge: You'd sniff that, not hear it. Which line makes a noise?

show.text: The benches were sticky with sauce.
show.nudge: You'd feel that on your skin. Which line makes a noise?

steps.ask: Tap the line you could hear.
steps.win: Yes! Humming and slurping are sounds. Check the other labels.

steps.say: Writers forget smell most. Here's the pool.

show.nudge: You'd hear that one. Which line could you sniff?
You'd feel that one on your skin. Which line could you sniff?

show.text: The air stank of chlorine and hot chips.

steps.win: Yes! Chlorine and hot chips. Details you sense are sensory details.

steps.say: Careful! Zed's line says smelled. Is that a smell detail?

options.reason: It is! Sniffing is a sense. Look at the last word.
Short is fine. 'It stank of burnt toast' is short too. What's missing?

options.text: It doesn't say what it smelled of.

steps.win: Yes! Nice is an opinion. Name the smell, like burnt toast.

steps.say: Fixing my first try: same canteen, senses other than sight.

show.text: The canteen was big and had lots of tables.

steps.ask: Which line puts you inside the canteen?

options.text: The canteen was very, very big and nice.
options.reason: Very big is still sight, and nice is an opinion. Can you smell or feel anything?

options.text: The canteen stank of burnt toast, and the benches were sticky with sauce.
The canteen had tables, chairs and a big blue door.
options.reason: That's a list of things to see. Is there a smell or a feel?

steps.win: Yes! A smell and a touch. Now you're in there.

steps.say: Zed says all five senses in one line is best.

show.text: I heard, smelt, tasted, touched and saw the noisy, smelly, salty, sticky, shiny beach.

steps.ask: What's the problem with Zed's line?

options.reason: Count them! It uses all five. Is it easy to picture?

options.text: Too many senses at once. You can't picture any of them.

options.reason: Beaches are great places to write about. Count how many senses are in one line.

steps.win: Yes! Two or three senses is plenty.

terms.means: What you see. Good, but add another sense too.
What you hear, like whistles shrieking or kids slurping.
What you sniff. Say what it smells of, not just 'nice'.
What your skin feels: hot, sticky, scratchy or freezing.

examples.text: The canteen hummed with kids slurping noodles,
the benches were sticky with sauce.

card.test: Cover the sight words. Can you still hear, smell or feel the place? If not, add one.

weDo.frame: Indi is painting the footy change room, but she needs words first.
weDo.prompt: Which sentence puts you inside the change room?
weDo.hint: Which one could you smell and feel?
weDo.success: Sweaty socks give a smell, and the gritty floor gives touch. You're standing right there.

options.text: The change room reeked of sweaty socks, and the floor was cold and gritty under our feet.
The change room had rows of blue lockers, and a faded team photo hung above the benches.
options.reason: Lockers and a team photo are things you see. Can you smell, hear or feel anything?

options.text: The change room was the most disgusting room in the whole school, and we all hated it.
options.reason: Disgusting is an opinion. It doesn't give the reader a smell, a sound or a touch.

weDo.frame: Indi needs one sentence about the school canteen before she paints it.
weDo.prompt: Build a canteen sentence with a smell and a touch in it.
weDo.hint: Which tile could you sniff? Which could you feel?
weDo.success: Burnt toast is a smell, and sticky benches are a touch. Now we're standing in the canteen.

tiles: and the benches were sticky with sauce.
and the menu board was bright orange.
accept: The canteen stank of burnt toast and the benches were sticky with sauce.
body.reason: Find a smell tile and a touch tile. A counter and a menu board are only things you see.

creature.name: Plumoth
creature.blurb: A moth with feathery feelers that can taste the air and hear a leaf land. It flutters close to any place that's described well.

workshop.mentor: The pool was loud before we even got there: whistles shrieking, little kids howling, someone's dad doing a bomb that sounded like a fridge falling off a truck. The air stank of chlorine and hot chips. I stepped onto the concrete and hopped straight off again, because it burnt the soles of my feet. When I finally jumped in, the water was so cold it punched the breath out of me.
workshop.ask:
Write four sentences about one place, using two or three senses.
Stuck? Start with: 'The first thing I smelt was...'
Challenge: never say what anything looks like.
checklist: I used two or three senses, not just sight.
I can point to a sound and a smell.
My smell or sound could only belong to this place.
I swapped one blurry word (nice, good, big).
